Every year I am amazed at what these teachers do daily and accomplish with our children annually. Mrs. Adams, two of my children’s kindergarten teacher, has been exceptional. articles.text: Editor: Moving to Piedmont more than 20 years ago was handsdown the best decision we ever made for our family. In addition to the beautiful homes, parks, and playgrounds, Piedmont has a renewable resource that makes it punch far above its weight: a small army of committed, competent, empathetic and smart volunteers who step up to help guide decision making for our town. Conna McCarthy is a poster child for that army. As a member of the City Council for the past four years, Conna has shown a deep commitment to listen to every member of the Piedmont community, and to transparency and accountability for the decisions made by the City Council that greatly impact the quality of life and safety of the town we all love. As owners of one of Piedmont’s most visible businesses, it’s important to us that the City Council is made up of dedicated volunteers who will put public service ahead of politics and ensure everyone in our community has a voice in important decisions. Over the years, we have both spent countless hours volunteering, parcel-tax wrangling, and event chairing in Piedmont. Or at least to us it felt like countless hours, until we noticed that every single time we were involved in a city-wide effort, Conna was there with us in the trenches, working to ensure our city and our schools thrived. She’s been a part of each and every initiative that makes Piedmont so special, from Tri-School fundraisers to the Piedmont Educational Foundation to securing pickleball in our town. We believe in Conna’s intelligence, empathy, humility and work ethic, and we urge you to relect her to the City Council on November 5th. –Laura Pochop & Chad Olcott She will come on board ready to work, without a learning curve. Lynda has had a constant, passionate involvement with her community and the environment, both in her career as a scientist and in her everyday life. Her life’s work is to preserve the environment and educate the youth. There is no one else who can match the qualifications needed for this job other than Lynda Deschambault. articles.text: I have known Conna McCarthy since our children were in Piedmont Middle School and we were both on the Parent Board. Since then we have worked together on many, many projects and many, many campaigns. Conna is a real people person and she cares deeply about our Piedmont community. She is an enthusiastic and tireless worker and has an impressive resume. But what sets Conna apart is her willingness to roll up her sleeves and dive right in. Thanks to Conna’s leadership on the Seismic Safety Campaign, our schools are much safer. Thanks to Conna’s extensive experience with the Piedmont Education Foundation, she understands how important the City/School relationship is. Thanks to Conna’s role on the Piedmont Recreation Commission, our city has improved pickleball courts. And thanks to Conna’s four years on our City Council, Piedmont is better positioned for the future. She asks the tough questions and makes the tough decisions, always guided by her smarts, true moral compass, and love of Piedmont. –Andrea Swenson Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Matt Simons Margaret “Maggie” Kane celebrated her 100th birthday in Piedmont over the weekend surrounded by friends, family and neighbors. Kane hosted a tea party prior to the birthday festivities at her home on Sunday, September 29, celebrating a century of life experiences, family ties and community bonds. Born on October 2, 1924, she grew up in Phoenixville outside of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, with her younger siblings Jimmy and Helen. Her father owned a thriving taxi business, but opportunities were “extremely limited” in the small manufacturing town. She recalled that Phoenixville was home to both a steel mill and a Goodyear rubber plant that offered steady employment, though she eschewed the restricted and physically laborious roles to follow in her parents footsteps and pursue higher education. When it came time for college, she decided to study public relations; a decision she credits to an uncle who lived and worked in the Bay Area. “He was here in San Francisco, and he was quite wellknown and a delightful guy,” Kane said. “And I thought, ‘that’s what I want to do.’ I mean, he was enjoying life to the hilt.” Kane said she remembers her uncle interviewing and socializing with a variety of personalities such as swimmer and actress Esther Williams and radio personality Major Bowes. Her uncle’s gregarious personality and career allowed him to lead an exciting life that she found inspiring. “He was very sharp and he just gravitated to people that were on his intellectual level,” Kane said. Kane attended the Charles Morris Price School of Advertising and Journalism in Philadelphia, where she earned her degree in one year by going to school at night and by day. She graduated in 1944, during World War II. She added the ongoing military draft at the time meant many opportunities that were previously dominated by men had been made available to women. She landed her first job at a print shop in Philadelphia. “I was the only woman they’d ever hired,” Kane said. However, Kane quickly became bored with the setup in Philadelphia and pined for something more. “There were no other women to have lunch with, and there Photos by Johan Quie The Kane residence ready to celebrate a centennial birthday party One-hundred-year-old Maggie Kane celebrating with her one-year-old next door neighbor Berit Quie Maggie Kane blows out candles on her birthday cake. Maggie Kane hosts a tea party for her friends and family. was nobody who was going to give you the time of day,” Kane said. “So I decided I better look around and find something more interesting.” Kane held a number of jobs between 1944 and 1950 and before the Korean War. Kane was hired at a Philadelphia advertising agency, where she discovered on her first day that one of her new colleagues was one of the many enlisted men who had returned from service. “I came in, and lo and behold, there’s a young man who had just been hired and had just returned from the Navy,” Kane recalled. His name was Bill Kane. Little did I know that he was going to be very much in my future.” The two dated for a year-anda-half, during which time he proposed to her on numerous occasions. “One day he came with a diamond ring that was his grandmother’s.” She said she worried that refusing the ring would embarrass him, so she decided to keep the ring for a couple of weeks before returning it to him. “I never gave it back,” Kane said with a smile. They were engaged in 1952 and married the next year. They moved into a brownstone apartment in Philadelphia, and raised a family of five children, Coleman, Lachlann, Nevan, Michael and Caroline. “But we thought with five children to put through college, we’d better get to California,” Kane said. “The state had a reputation that it was so inexpensive to go to college. So we packed them up and out we came.” Kane and her family moved to Piedmont in 1972 for the school systems, and she has been here ever since. articles.text: As a senior in high school, in the thick of applying to college, balancing homework, being an active member of multiple extracurriculars, and just in general stressed, I forget to breathe. Sometimes I am so focused on what I’m doing, I lose focus of myself. and of what truly matters. For each person, what truly matters is different. For me it’s being a good friend, family member, singer, athlete, and more. Remembering these things and people helps me feel like myself again. Recently I have felt that I’ve been pulled in so many different directions I don’t feel like myself. I don’t feel like a good friend, or like a good daughter. I feel like I’m getting stripped of who I am because people keep telling me who I’m supposed to be and what I’m supposed to do. I don’t like that – I really don’t. I want to be able to decide on my own. Being told that I might not have that choice is heartbreaking. We are all so stretched thin by responsibilities and expectations, we can’t always see the similarities of our situations. I am being faced with the reality that I have to say goodbye to many parts of myself this year. I am saying goodbye to being a high school student and athlete. I am saying goodbye to being a part of a choir that I’ve called home for 14 years. I am saying goodbye to my best friend as she moves away for college. I am saying goodbye to my childhood. I know that seniors have been faced with that question a lot recently. The question of who are we? What will we do? And we are being forced to choose now, when we ourselves are still trying to figure it out. I am scared. Because if I don’t even know who I am, how am I supposed to convince someone else who I am? I recently heard a quote that helped bring me clarity through the fog of my own uncertainty. It went something like this: “I am at a point in my life where I am letting go of things that don’t serve me anymore. And letting go of some of that stuff, I am going to leave claw marks, because I love those things and those people.” I will let go of my childhood because dwelling on the fact that it’s over doesn’t serve me. I will let go of my uncertainty about who I will become, because being scared about it doesn’t serve me. I will let go of my best friend because I can’t make her stay and stop her from finding out who she is going to be and it won’t serve either of us. And I will let go of people telling me who I’m supposed to be because that is meant for me to find out. But I am excited, to see who I will be in six months after I’ve let go and started fresh, because something about meeting a new, happier version of myself is beautiful. As we – especially seniors – are faced with never ending existential questions about our lives, the threat of losing ourselves trying to be someone we’re not for somebody or something else, and the constant letting go, I ask that we remember that we are just starting on our own adventures. That we will end up where we are supposed to be. That we will be OK. That it’s just one day at a time, until we have the courage to look past today and into tomorrow. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and a student at Bentley High School ln Lafayette.

articles.text: Ariel Rodriguez Many high schools throughout the country will be hosting the PSAT this month, but what is the PSAT? PSAT stands for Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test, essentially the precursor to the SAT. Like the SAT, the PSAT is a digital, adaptive test that includes a Reading & Writing section and a Math section. Both the SAT and PSAT are 2 hours and 14 minutes long. There are also some major differences between the PSAT and the SAT. The PSAT is only offered once per year, in October, and is typically hosted by your high school. The SAT, on the other hand, is offered seven times per year at test centers throughout the country. The maximum scaled score on each section of the PSAT is 760; the maximum scaled score on each section of the SAT is 800. If you are a junior taking the PSAT, your scores could qualify you for National Merit Commendation or National Merit Semifinalist. Many schools will also allow sophomores to take the PSAT, but only scores from junior year can qualify for national merit recognition. Exact score cutoffs are determined by state in the year following the PSAT taken. So, a junior taking the PSAT Fall 2024 will not find out if they have received national merit commendation or semifinalist status until 2025. Commended students are typically within the top 3-4% of testers; semifinalists are typically within the top 1% of testers. Historically, California has been one of the states with the highest cutoffs. Students who are National Merit Semifinalists can apply to become National Merit Scholars. National Merit Scholar status makes you eligible for different scholarships: some from the National Merit Corporation, some from private corporations, and others from colleges and universities themselves. While there are some perks for students who score in the top percentiles on the PSAT, for the vast majority of students, the PSAT mainly functions as a practice test. If the PSAT is being offered at your school, go ahead and take it and put in a good faith effort, but don’t put undue stress on this test. Instead, use it as an opportunity to gain more information that will empower you to understand how standardized tests may become part of the bigger picture for college admissions. I am saying goodbye to being a part of a choir that I’ve called home for 14 years. I am saying goodbye to my best friend as she moves away for college. I am saying goodbye to my childhood. I know that seniors have been faced with that question a lot recently. The question of who are we? What will we do? And we are being forced to choose now, when we ourselves are still trying to figure it out. I am scared. Because if I don’t even know who I am, how am I supposed to convince someone else who I am? I recently heard a quote that helped bring me clarity through the fog of my own uncertainty. It went something like this: “I am at a point in my life where I am letting go of things that don’t serve me anymore. And letting go of some of that stuff, I am going to leave claw marks, because I love those things and those people.” I will let go of my childhood because dwelling on the fact that it’s over doesn’t serve me. I will let go of my uncertainty about who I will become, because being scared about it doesn’t serve me. I will let go of my best friend because I can’t make her stay and stop her from finding out who she is going to be and it won’t serve either of us. And I will let go of people telling me who I’m supposed to be because that is meant for me to find out. But I am excited, to see who I will be in six months after I’ve let go and started fresh, because something about meeting a new, happier version of myself is beautiful. As we – especially seniors – are faced with never ending existential questions about our lives, the threat of losing ourselves trying to be someone we’re not for somebody or something else, and the constant letting go, I ask that we remember that we are just starting on our own adventures. That we will end up where we are supposed to be. That we will be OK. That it’s just one day at a time, until we have the courage to look past today and into tomorrow. Thinking Outside the Classroom Putting the PSAT into Perspective By Emily Thompson and Ariel Rodriguez Many high schools throughout the country will be hosting the PSAT this month, but what is the PSAT? PSAT stands for Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test, essentially the precursor to the SAT. Like the SAT, the PSAT is a digital, adaptive test that includes a Reading & Writing section and a Math section. Both the SAT and PSAT are 2 hours and 14 minutes long. There are also some major differences between the PSAT and the SAT. The PSAT is only offered once per year, in October, and is typically hosted by your high school. The SAT, on the other hand, is offered seven times per year at test centers throughout the country. The maximum scaled score on each section of the PSAT is 760; the maximum scaled score on each section of the SAT is 800. If you are a junior taking the PSAT, your scores could qualify you for National Merit Commendation or National Merit Semifinalist. Many schools will also allow sophomores to take the PSAT, but only scores from junior year can qualify for national merit recognition. Exact score cutoffs are determined by state in the year following the PSAT taken. So, a junior taking the PSAT Fall 2024 will not find out if they have received national merit commendation or semifinalist status until 2025. Commended students are typically within the top 3-4% of testers; semifinalists are typically within the top 1% of testers. Historically, California has been one of the states with the highest cutoffs. Students who are National Merit Semifinalists can apply to become National Merit Scholars. National Merit Scholar status makes you eligible for different scholarships: some from the National Merit Corporation, some from private corporations, and others from colleges and universities themselves. While there are some perks for students who score in the top percentiles on the PSAT, for the vast majority of students, the PSAT mainly functions as a practice test. If the PSAT is being offered at your school, go ahead and take it and put in a good faith effort, but don’t put undue stress on this test. Instead, use it as an opportunity to gain more information that will empower you to understand how standardized tests may become part of the bigger picture for college admissions. articles.text: Scouts and parents pause after completing a climb to an altitude of 9381 feet. Pictured are Leo Kansal, Joelle Frechet, Liam King, Charlie Robinson, Tom Robinson, Alex Wolff, and Dante Rodriguez. Three Scouts, including two Eagles, and five adults from Piedmont Troop 4 went on a 50-mile backpacking trip last summer in Desolation Wilderness, a mountainous area near Lake Tahoe. Members of the troop prepared for months in advance to make sure they were prepared for any situation. Overall, the trip was a great success, helped a lot by Troop 4’s Dante Rodriguez, who has led plenty of 50 Milers as a Scout with Troop 4 and now as an adult. The Scouts were well prepared for challenges, including rain, heat, and cold. A typical day on the trip started with breakfast. Breakfasts ranged from granola with dehydrated milk to oatmeal and dried blueberries, but they felt special to be eating in such beautiful places. The day would continue with several miles of hiking, a good view, and a stop for lunch at a place with shade and fresh water to filter. After lunch the Scouts would be back on the trail for a few more miles, before setting up camp for the night. In the afternoon the Scouts would often take a swim in a lake, lay on the warm rocks, and enjoy the beautiful scenery that can only be found in the mountains of the Sierra Nevada range. The crystal clear lakes in the mountainous forests were not warm but were not frigid. As the sun began to set, the Scouts began preparing dinner and would eat their evening meal sitting on warm rocks at their campsite. But as the sun dips behind the horizon, the mosquitoes come out. Scouts have many methods of sleeping outdoors – some choose hammocks, some sleep under the stars on tarps, while others use tents. The important part is getting rested for the next day’s adventure and reducing the weight you carry as much as possible. Some of the most memorable parts of the 50-mile hike were going over Dick’s Pass, eating dinner on the rocks at Middle Velma Lake, swimming at Lake Ropi, and seeing a water snake at Lake of the Woods. On a trip like this, water is important and the Scouts almost always stopped at a lake for lunch and camped at a lake every night. In total the trip took seven days and reached an elevation of 9381 feet. Troop 4 Scouts hike up a valley to reach a lake where they set up camp for the night. Some Scouts chose to use hammocks because for one person they are lighter than tents. Leo Kansal, Liam King and Alex Wolff at Clyde Lake Scouts put on their rain gear when it started raining on the last night of the trip.

articles.text: Dozens of pickleball enthusiasts converged on the middle school courts on Saturday, September 21, to play in a fund-raising tournament to support the school district’s Wellness Center. The “Positively Pickled” tournament proved to be so popular that organizers had to create a waitlist to accommodate would-be entrants. More than $65,000 was generated by the tournament through family and corporate donations, all in support of the Wellness Center, which provides counseling and mental health services to Piedmont students in high school and middle school. Last year the Wellness Center provided more than 2,000 therapy sessions to Piedmont students. The inaugural Wellness Center tournament included beginPickleball enthusiasts Shyla Ranga, Paige Rampton, Madeleine Ewen, Mackenzie Ewen, and Grace Fa at the Wellness Center pickleball tournament Intermediate division winners Reed and Aaron Bennett ner, intermediate and competitive divisions. Twenty-eight intermediate and 12 competitive division teams participated. Father-son duo Reed and Aaron Bennett won the intermediate division, followed by runners-up Cindy and Kris Lynds. Ray Ramillosa and Stefan Schulze won the competitive division, with Beth Barrett and Virginia Davis a close second. For many players, it was their first time participating in a pickleball tournament. Before beginning play, new players received a group lesson from professional pickleball player Carolyn Wei. Coaches advised beginners on scoring and rules. Montclair Sports Tennis & Pickleball donated 10 pickleball rackets to the first five doubles teams registered in the beginners division. “There was a lot of learning and joy on the court,” said tournament chair, Blair Paige. “It really showed how people of all ages can play pickleball together and have fun.” The winners of the intermediate and competitive divisions received $100 Mulberry’s Market gift certificates, and runners-up were awarded $50 gift certificates from Yellow Door in Montclair. Giant jars of pickles served as both trophies and fun photo opportunities. Major corporate donors included Elfster and TPG. In-kind donors included Montclair Sports Tennis & Pickleball, Mulberry’s Market, Yellow Door, and Bay Padel. “It’s so representative of our amazing Piedmont community that people don’t just give for academics but also to support our student’s mental wellness,” said Wellness Center Support Committee chair Neha Gupta. “Student mental health should be prioritized just as much as the library, the arts, and sports,” Gupta added. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department hosted its sixth annual Car Show on Saturday, September 21, with hot coffee and even hotter automobiles parked in front of the Exedra. Piedmont Police Officer Tyler Petit once again led the event which has brought cops, coffee and cars to the center of Piedmont as a part of the department’s outreach efforts. The Car Show took place on the last day of summer, which turned out to be a beautiful Saturday morning in Piedmont. Around 85 vintage, classic and muscle cars were on display for public viewing. Upwards of 500 viewers came out for a cup of coffee, chat with a car owners, and to witness a cornucopia of chrome. “When we start throwing these events people get to know us,” said Petit. “It’s not Officer Petit its ‘hey, Tyler.’ For me, as a police officer and someone who wants this kind of customer service in a community, I like to know that people can come to me as a friend.” The set up was slightly different this year because of the ongoing construction at the Piedmont Police Department of a new dispatch center, scheduled to be completed in April 2025. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ flag football team wrapped up a successful week with two wins out of its last three games. It started with a 14-12 win over San Leandro at Witter Field on Tuesday, September 24 then followed with a 19-14 win over Hayward on the Farmers’ home field two days later. The wins were bookended by a 32-0 loss at Berkeley on Monday, September 30, but the result is accompanied with an asterisk. After Berkeley provided the wrong starting time for Monday’s game, PHS was forced to promote a collection of Junior Varsity players to their Varsity starting lineup. “On our schedule it was 5:30 p.m. and we wound up losing half the varsity squad and JV stepped up. We played tonight with a totally new group. It’s not an excuse, but that was the circumstances,” coach Beth Black said. Piedmont’s wins over San Leandro and Hayward started its first win streak of the season. PHS will get one more chance with Berkeley in the regular-season finale on October 24. Despite the loss, JV call-up Riley Burton showed she might be ready for the varsity, leading the Highlanders offensively as a running back and receiver, and recording runs of 13, 18, and a 33 yards. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team suffered a 3-0 loss to Alameda. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team took a 3-0 loss on the road to Alameda on Wednesday, September 25 by scores of 25-8, 25-8, 25-13. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 1-9 entering the final month of play with eight matches left. Piedmont now looks ahead to visiting Western Alameda County Conference powerhouse, Bishop O’Dowd, next Tuesday, October 8. Game Recap In the first set, Piedmont got out to a quick 3-2 lead with kills by Hanley Carling, but the set quickly unraveled. At that point, Alameda went on a 10-0 scoring run to jump ahead 12-3 before Piedmont’s Stella Wilk scored a kill. After that, Alameda scored 10 of the next 12 points, including four kills and three aces. Fiona Olsen scored a kill, but alameda finished the set with three straight point. Piedmont similarly won the opening two points of the second set thanks to a kill by Carling and an error by the Hornets. The two sides traded points, including kills by Wilks and Carling, until Alameda held a one-point 7-6 lead. That’s when the Hornets went on another exhausting scoring run, landing eight straight points before Carling scored another spike. Following that, Alameda scored another nine straight points including five kills and two aces. Carling got one more kill before the close of the second set. The Highlanders were competitive for the first half of the third set before falling behind. Piedmont actually battled to an 8-7 lead thanks to kills by Carling, #11 and Sophie Glass, and an ace by Charli Panico. PHS only briefly held the advantage when the Hornets went on a three point scoring run to go up 11-8. PHS then scored two points to cut the deficit to one point at 11-10, but the Hornets then went on another long-lasting streak of points. Alameda scored 11 straight points with four kills and four aces to their credit to go up 22-10. Piedmont’s Olsen and Wilks slammed in spikes to give Piedmont two straight points, but Alameda closed the game with a pair of kills of its own. Final stats: Carling had seven kills, Olsen had two kills, Wilk had four, Julia Stokes had one block, Panico had one ace. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-9 overall, 0-2 league) will play at Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 8 at 6:30 p.m. Hanley Carling (5) had six kills against Alameda. Also pictured is Allyson Huynh. Stella Wilk had four kills against the Hornets.

Piedmont now looks ahead to visiting Western Alameda County Conference powerhouse, Bishop O’Dowd, next Tuesday, October 8. At that point, Alameda went on a 10-0 scoring run to jump ahead 12-3 before Piedmont’s Stella Wilk scored a kill. After that, Alameda scored 10 of the next 12 points, including four kills and three aces. Fiona Olsen scored a kill, but alameda finished the set with three straight point. Piedmont similarly won the opening two points of the second set thanks to a kill by Carling and an error by the Hornets. The two sides traded points, including kills by Wilks and Carling, until Alameda held a one-point 7-6 lead. That’s when the Hornets went on another exhausting scoring run, landing eight straight points before Carling scored another spike. Following that, Alameda scored another nine straight points including five kills and two aces. Carling got one more kill before the close of the second set. The Highlanders were competitive for the first half of the third set before falling behind. Piedmont actually battled to an 8-7 lead thanks to kills by Carling, #11 and Sophie Glass, and an ace by Charli Panico. PHS only briefly held the advantage when the Hornets went on a three point scoring run to go up 11-8. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team finished a rough week with two defeats. Most recently, they fell 5-2 to Alameda at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Thursday, September 26 after losing 6-1 at Marin Academy in San Rafael the previous day. Their loss to Alameda comes against a Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division rival. Two of Piedmont’s losses came down to tightly contested three-set matches. Three of their losses to Marin Academy also went to three sets. The Highlanders will get one more chance to defeat Alameda on October 23. “Against Marin Academy, three matches went to third set tiebreaks. Despite winning the first set in each, we lost all of them,” said coach Jim Landes. “We need to avoid letting up after a first set win. With Alameda, four matches went to the third set and we split them. Again, we need to fight against relaxing too much after a good start,” coach Jim Landes said. In the match with Alameda, Piedmont won one singles and one doubles match. Maddie Tran and Emma Chan won their No. 2 match after trailing in the first set and third set, but claimed the win after their opponents had to forfeit the match with the final set tied at 5-5. Tran and Chan won 7-5, 3-6, 5-5 (retire), but were trailing 5-2 in both the first and third sets before mounting momentous comebacks. “We were losing 2-5 in the first set and our mental game was so bad, then we started winning games and building momentum to win the set. It was almost the same in the third set where we went down 2-5. We were thinking back to the first set and knew we could do it again. We brought it back to 5-all and had momentum going again,” Tran said. “A lot of my first serves were going out. In the third set, I started hitting my serves really hard and landing them. We started getting a lot of points when I was landing my first serves. Maddie’s volleys in front of the net were also really good. She was hitting them to where they couldn’t get it,” Chan mentioned. articles.text: AXIS Dance Company, an acclaimed ensemble of disabled and neurodiverse dancers, will perform Friday through Sunday, October 11-13 at San Francisco’s ODC Theater. The Bay Area-based dance company was founded in 1987 and has performed in more than 100 cities in the U.S., the United Kingdom, Europe and the United Arab Emirates. The company’s mission is to create world-class productions that challenge perceptions and redefine dance and disability. AXIS will perform new choreography for its home season Ecos, with Berkeley-based contemporary dance company, Post:ballet, serving as special guests. “Ecos brings together extraordinary artists to explore the complexities of our shared human experience,” said AXIS Dance Company Artistic Director Nadia Adame. “Each piece in this Home Season reflects a unique perspective, yet together they resonate with a powerful, collective spirit. This season is a heartfelt invitation to connect, reflect, and be moved together.” Tickets for Ecos are available now at www.axisdance.org. AXIS Dance Company artists perform onstage.

articles.text: Victoria Hurd will perform a piano concert on Sunday, October 29 at Plymouth Church, 424 Monte Vista Avenue. Titled Beethoven Revisited, the concert will start at 5:30 p.m. It is a benefit for SAVETHECHILDREN.ORG Beethoven Revisited focuses on Beethoven’s pianistic use of the sustaining pedal. He didn’t have one! (He did occasionally use a knee lever to sustain one chord.) Modern pianos sound bare without the pedal, so the concert will adapt early piano techniques to the resonant, powerful sound of modern pianos. Included in the program, for historical context, will be music by Mozart and Chopin. Victoria Hurd studied Performance Practices as a graduate at Stanford University and has played piano and harpsichord for many years. She infuses her playing with a love of dance and song; She also sings with Chora Nova in Berkeley. Admission is your donation receipt to: https://bit.ly/VHurdBeethoven. Pianist Victoria Hurd ®

articles.text: Performances scheduled for November 8-17 Opera Parallèle will open its 2024-25 season with its firstever production at the California Academy of Sciences Planetarium om Golden Gate Park from November 8 through 17. Entitled Everest: Opera in the Planetarium, the production is based on the internationally renowned opera, Everest, composed by Joby Talbot with a libretto by Gene Scheer. The oneact opera retells the 1996 Mount Everest disaster, when several mountaineers died after a severe storm hit during their climb to the summit. It is based on interviews with survivors and shows in the deaths of mountaineers Rob Hall and Doug Hanse. Opera Parallèle’s production uses the Academy of Sciences’ state-of-the-art planetarium to present the opera in bold new iteration. The event is not a live opera, but an immersive operatic experience. Award winning conductor Nicole Paiement leads the orchestra as animations come to life through facial tracking technology. The cast includes features Sasha Cooke, mezzo-soprano; Nathan Granner, tenor; Kevin California Academy of Sciences Planetarium Burdette, bass; Hadleigh Adams, baritone; Charlotte Fanvu, treble; Matt Boehler, bass; Shawnette Sulker, soprano; Whitney Steele, mezzo-soprano; and Kevin Gino, tenor. The launch of the company’s 2024-25 season also coincides with Opera Parallele’s 15th anniversary. “When we launched Opera Parallèle, we knew we were creating something that had the capacity to change the perception of opera as an art form and storytelling mechanism,” explained Artistic Director Nicole Paiement. “After 15 years of pushing artistic boundaries through partnerships with many hundreds of talented and diverse creative collaborators, singers, composers, and musicians, the world of opera has indeed become more varied, more relevant, more innovative. I am very proud that Opera Parallèle has been recognized as a catalyst in that shift.” Everest: Opera at the Planetarium begins Friday, November 8 at 6.30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.cityboxoffice.com/ everest.
articles.title: Opera Parallèle launches season with Everest: Opera in the Planetarium

articles.text: Kedrick Armstrong will lead the Oakland Symphony on October 18 in his debut as the symphony’s ninth music director. Ar mstrong’s unanimous appointment to the position in April marked the end of a twoyear search since the passing of the symphony’s previous conductor Michael Morgan in August 2021. Before Armstrong’s appointment, the symphony invited a series of guest conductors. “The search committee… was impressed by Armstrong’s demonstrated leadership and community-building abilities along with his passion for and command of an extraordinarily broad range of music,” said publicist Marshall Lam. “All of these qualities were reflected in the programs that he conceived, organized and conducted with the Oakland Symphony.” Armstrong, 30, grew up in Georgetown, South Carolina and established his music career in Chicago. Prior to being named music director in Oakland, he worked as the creative partner and principal conductor of the Knox-Galesburg Symphony in Illinois. Armstrong was named by the Washington Post as one of the “Top 22 Composers and Performers to Watch” in 2022. Armstrong was a guest conductor with Oakland Symphony in 2022 for the Summer Stage at Oakland City Hall, then again in 2023 and early 2024. His new job as music director prompted him to permanently move to the East Bay in August. “The Oakland Symphony community has embraced me with open arms since my first visit. It immediately felt like a place I wanted to call home,” Armstrong said. In his new role, Armstrong will conduct the orchestra’s concerts in and around the Bay Area, participate in the organization’s education and community engagement programs, and be the symphony’s cultural ambassador to Bay Area artists and communities. “Living in the Bay Area now, it’s learning a new community, learning a new area, learning what interests people with cultural items that are significant to the Bay,” said Armstrong. The position with Oakland Symphony is unique in part because the post has long been held by Black conductors, Michael Morgan and Calvin Simmons, who combined led the symphony for more than 40 Photos by Scott Chernis Before he was appointed to his new role, Armstrong was a guest conductor with Oakland Symphony between 2022 and 2024. Photos by Scott Chernis Kedrick Armstrong established his career in Chicago before he was named Music Director for the Oakland Symphony. years. “As an African-American conductor, I find it humbling to stand on the shoulders of both Michael Morgan and Calvin Simmons,” Armstrong said. “Having that legacy of both Simmons and Morgan has been empowering for me. But also it makes it so that my vision and my goals are aligned with the history of this organization.” Armstrong said his experience with the Oakland Symphony has reiterated the strength of the bonds present in classical music. “There are beautiful differences and similarities; one of the similarities is just kind of how tight knit it is,” he said. “On a national scale you realize in classical music just how small the world is and how much we all know each other. I’m trying to learn more about this deep history. I also want to bring everything that I have as a 30-year-old. I pinch myself every day. I truly feel like one of the luckiest people to be able to do this work.” Armstrong’s inaugural performance as music director with the Oakland Symphony will be on Friday, October 18 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland.

articles.text: Kristen Stewart and Julianne Moore in Still Alice Life is fragile, tenuous, and each day is a gamble. Until it isn’t. The idea that bad things happen to good people is an abstraction… and suddenly what we took for granted – another dawn, and all that follows – can no longer hold our weight, like fragile ice on a winter’s pond. Still Alice is about such a life and may be more truth than some viewers want to confront in a film, due in great part to a tour de force performance by Julianne Moore. She portrays Dr. Alice Howland, a professor of linguistics at Colombia University, married to John (Alec Baldwin), a research scientist and the mother of three lovely children (Kristen Stewart, Kate Bosworth and Hunter Parrish). Alice accomplished, cherished by her family and colleagues, just 50, and relishing in every way this moment in her life. But ever so gradually she begins to notice small moments when her memory hits a speed bump and what was automatic eludes her. And so begins a cruel and insidious journey, one in which all that she is, all that she has become, begins to abandon her. With John she visits a neurologist who confirms that she has familial early onset Alzheimer’s disease. It’s a betrayal of her mind that is unexpected and will be, with unyielding certainty, catastrophic and like a flower in full bloom, every pedal vibrant with life, she begins to close ever so slowly. What is so insidious, so tragic, is that Alice – bright, scholarly, educated, loving – is told in detail what awaits her, the path that stretches before her is detailed, like a photograph of familiar colors and images left out in the sunshine that slowly begins to fade. The irony of the film is its title: Still Alice. From the moment of her diagnosis, when she is told that the disease she has is very rare and also genetic (it’s possible that the gene she inherited came from her father, an alcoholic, and she may have passed it on to her children), Alice is no longer still Alice. She is now that person who struggles to find the courage and grace to face each day, to suffer each moment of forgetfulness, clinging to any remnant of who she was and wishes she still could be. Though this subject matter is not unique, what gives Still Alice its deeply human essence is the resonating performance by Julianne Moore, who was nominated for an Oscar as Best Actress. She is remarkable and restrained. The camera lingers on her in tight, intimate shots, her every feature conveying the hope and sheer terror and brief moments of panic and lucidity that are now her life’s experiences. Moore is astonishing. She is just so good. As is the film, which is never gratuitous or maudlin. Still Alice. Directed by Richard Glatzer. Starring Alec Baldwin, Julianne Moore, Kristen Stewart. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG-13. Released ln 2014. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/ MAX/apple tv.

articles.text: If you are exploring the extraordinary works of Studio Ghibli, you have discovered that the lead character is often a young female who is simultaneously fragile and fearless. When Marnie Was There is based on the 1967 fantasy book by English author Joan G. Robinson. The film’s protagonist is a lonely, androgynous 12-yearold girl named Anna (Kiernan Shipka) who lives in urban Sapporo, Japan. Because she is asthmatic, her foster mother, Mrs. Kadoya (Kathy Bates), sends her to live with relatives in the country – a windswept, marshy, seaside area that will, hopefully, restore Anna’s health. While exploring the marshes, Anna unexpectedly comes across a deserted mansion that seems eerily familiar. It’s there that she encounters a strange, mysterious girl of her own age, very western looking, with striking blonde hair and wearing out-of-date clothes. Unexpectedly, the two develop a friendship and begin to share dreams and diaries which, for Anna, lead to moments of self-discovery and revelation. Architects want their roof designs to look good, but also not to leak! This is not always as easy as it seems. Complicated building forms and leak-risky layouts like decks over living spaces can make a dry building a challenge. In fact, the number one litigation issue architects and engineers face is water intrusion, i.e., leaks. The roof design process is therefore multi-faceted with structural and waterproofing considerations closely tied to aesthetics. In the roofing world, there are basically two kinds of roofs: sloped roofs and “flat” roofs, each with its own requirements and limitations. The park quickly became a popular spot for Sunday School picnics and school field trips. In the summer of 1882, a reported 5,000 to 7,000 passengers rode Blair’s horsecar per month. At the end of Highland Avenue, a large wooden arch spanned the entrance to the park. Admission was free to those who travelled in their own carriages, but there was a ten-cent fare to ride Blair’s horsecar. Benches near the lakes and picnic tables in shady nooks provided pleasant spots to picnic. There were even swings for children. No refreshments were available at Blair’s Park, and picnickers were encouraged to bring their own baskets. A lively stream cascaded down Moraga Canyon and spilled in a beautiful waterfall into the park. Rustic bridges crisscrossed the falls and stream. The more adventuresome could climb up to Inspiration Point on the knoll above Mountain View Cemetery. Young boys called it “Perspiration Point.” From this 700-foot elevation, hikers were rewarded with expansive views of Oakland, Alameda, Berkeley, San Francisco, the Golden Gate without a bridge, and Mt. Tamalpais. A spring provided fresh water for picnickers and hikers and is the probable namesake of Spring Path, just east of the Corporation Yard. Blair’s Park was a popular destination. After Walter Blair died in 1888, the park was purchased in 1890 by the company that would operate a cable car up Oakland Avenue. …But that’s another story. Today that lively stream and waterfall are under Coaches Field. Mountain View Cemetery bought the northern half of Blair’s Park, including the lakes. In 1917 and 1922, contractor Guy Taylor built houses on the southern half. Today, the name “Blair Park” continues to live on current maps of Piedmont. The City now calls the land on the south side of Moraga Avenue opposite Maxwelton Road “Blair Park.” Blair’s Park began as a picnic park where visitors came to enjoy being outdoors. It is fitting that today the tradition continues with the play field and baseball/ softball diamond at Coaches Field and the Kennelly Skate Park. articles.text: In the 1870s, Walter Blair was already a successful dairyman, quarryman and extensive land owner. Blair then turned his energy to transportation and developing horsecar lines. After partnering with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to the end of Piedmont Avenue, Blair built his own line in 1878. The Ride to Blair’s Park Blair’s Piedmont Railway began where the Piedmont Avenue line ended and travelled from the gates of Mountain View Cemetery, through Blair’s grain fields, up to Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) and on to the Piedmont Springs Hotel (currently Piedmont Park). Blair had the finest horsecar, with upholstered seats, a carpet on the floor and even a fringe on the top. He called it the “Palace Car.” It ran hourly and was the only public transportation to Piedmont. Lombardi In the 1870s, Walter Blair was already a successful dairyman, quarryman and extensive land owner. Blair then turned his energy to transportation and developing horsecar lines. After partnering with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to the end of Piedmont Avenue, Blair built his own line in 1878. The Ride to Blair’s Park Blair’s Piedmont Railway began where the Piedmont Avenue line ended and travelled from the gates of Mountain View Cemetery, through Blair’s grain fields, up to Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) and on to the Piedmont Springs Hotel (currently Piedmont Park). Blair had the finest horsecar, with upholstered seats, a carpet on the floor and even a fringe on the top. He called it the “Palace Car.” It ran hourly and was the only public transportation to Piedmont. Newspapers of the day described a ride on Blair’s horsecar as a pleasant even romantic one, winding through fields of grain and up hillsides with birds singing, brooks murmuring, balmy air and gentle breezes. Blair’s Park To increase the number of passengers on his Piedmont Railway, Blair created Blair’s Park where families could escape the dusty streets of downtown Oakland and “spend a pleasant day rambling in the country.” He developed 40 acres of his own land between Mountain View Cemetery and Moraga Road as a picnic park. He began by thinning out some of the eucalyptus trees that grew as a border between his land and the cemetery’s. (Some of Blair’s original eucalyptus trees still grow along the cemetery border near the lakes.) Blair graded pathways and built several bridges over the stream that ran through his park. The paths led picnickers along the stream, through the ravine and up the hillsides among trees and wildflowers. He also constructed several dams and created small lakes. (The lakes in Mountain View Cemetery date back to Blair’s Park.) Walter Blair dedicated his park on June 4, 1884, and the Oakland Daily Evening Tribune reported Walter Blair’s horsecars at the entrance to Blair’s Park, currently the corner of Highland and Moraga avenues. that “upwards of 400 people rambled through the delightful groves and wooded slopes, enjoying the beauties of nature and the magnificent scenery and views.” With visitors headed for Blair’s Park and the Piedmont Springs Hotel, newspapers soon reported that 700 to 800 passengers rode Walter Blair’s horsecar weekly. The park quickly became a popular spot for Sunday School picnics and school field trips. In the summer of 1882, a reported 5,000 to 7,000 passengers rode Blair’s horsecar per month. At the end of Highland Avenue, a large wooden arch spanned the entrance to the park. Admission was free to those who travelled in their own carriages, but there was a ten-cent fare to ride Blair’s horsecar. Benches near the lakes and picnic tables in shady nooks provided pleasant spots to picnic. There were even swings for children. No refreshments were available at Blair’s Park, and picnickers were encouraged to bring their own baskets. A lively stream cascaded down Moraga Canyon and spilled in a beautiful waterfall into the park. Rustic bridges crisscrossed the falls and stream. The more adventuresome could climb up to Inspiration Point on the knoll above Mountain View Cemetery. Young boys called it “Perspiration Point.” From this 700-foot elevation, hikers were rewarded with expansive views of Oakland, Alameda, Berkeley, San Francisco, the Golden Gate without a bridge, and Mt. Tamalpais. A spring provided fresh water for picnickers and hikers and is the probable namesake of Spring Path, just east of the Corporation Yard. Blair’s Park was a popular destination. After Walter Blair died in 1888, the park was purchased in 1890 by the company that would operate a cable car up Oakland Avenue. …But that’s another story. The City now calls the land on the south side of Moraga Avenue opposite Maxwelton Road “Blair Park.” Blair’s Park began as a picnic park where visitors came to enjoy being outdoors. It is fitting that today the tradition continues with the play field and baseball/ softball diamond at Coaches Field and the Kennelly Skate Park. Your plants are probably feeling the seasonal shift by dropping leaves and slowing production. With all the browning plant material, it’s the perfect time to start a low maintenance compost bin for the benefit of garden seasons to Hands down the easiest composting method is cold composting. This requires little work to set up, almost no monitoring, Cold composting requires little work and results in nutritious, and you end up with wonderfully nutritious compost in six months or sooner. Start by purchasing or building either a cedar wood or plastic compost bin. Next, grab your carbon and nitrogen plant materials. Think of carbon as any material that’s brown and crispy, including cardboard or scrap paper. For nitrogen you can think of greens, like fresh foliage clippings, or anything that’s wet. In your compost bin, add these materials in a two to one ratio of carbon to nitrogen until the bin is full. The best compost is made from an assortment of materials as opposed to all one plant. If your garden doesn’t produce enough scraps, ask a neighbor who uses organic practices if they don’t mind contributing plant material to your bin. Once your bin is full, add enough water to the pile so it feels like a wrung out sponge. We placed our compost bin near a garden hose for easy access. Then you simply turn it with a garden fork when you feel like it. If you want compost created in the next few months, turn your pile once a week with a spray of water. If you’re okay with waiting and like the idea of stress free composting, truly only turn it when you remember, such as every few weeks. If your bin starts to get smelly, that’s a sign there are too many greens, so add more carbonaceous material like dry leaves. If your materials aren’t breaking down and it feels dry, try supplementing with fresh green clippings and more water. Since this is a cold composting method, meaning your bin won’t heat up to temperatures that kill weed seeds and disease, avoid adding any diseased plants or weeds from the garden. My biggest tip for successful composting is just trusting the process. It’s decomposition so you really can’t mess up that bad. Even if your ratios are off, it’s an easy fix of adding more nitrogen or more carbon and waiting for them to break down. With this method, you should have dark, nutritious, earthy scented compost to use in your garden in six months. So if you start your bin now, you’ll have fresh homemade compost for your spring garden. Girl And Her Dog Farm is run by backyard farmer Michelle Docter in Albany. articles.text: Born in 1925, long time Piedmont resident Jim Meagher passed away in September 2024 at the age of 98. Born James Francis Meagher in Oakland, he was the youngest of three boys and grew up in an era where the milkman came in a horse drawn cart down Grand Avenue. In his early teens during the Great Depression Jim recalled that he would go door-to-door collecting coat hangers to sell for a penny or two. Always on the move Jim learned how to use a metal lathe at age 13 at Stonehurst Iron Works, and later was employed at age 16 in the family business, Independent Iron Works. He entered St. Mary’s High School in Berkeley and graduated with the class of 1943. Outside of school hours during WWII, “Jimmy” machined components for H.J. Kaiser’s Liberty Ships and was drafted as the war ended. He graduated from the University of California in Berkeley as a Mechanical Engineer in 1952 and started his career at San Francisco’s Hunter’s Point Shipyard. As a young man living on San Francisco’s Nob Hill, Jim was an equestrian and played polo in Golden Gate Park. Among his many interests were learning to sail and ski, and for many years he was a student of Judo. In 1953 Jim received his pilot’s license, becoming a twin-engine certified private pilot. Jim would tell colorful stories of his adventures, including flying to Pasadena to watch Cal in the 1959 Rose Bowl. In the mid-1950’s, Jim joined the family business and led notable projects for Independent Iron Works, including the James Lick Freeway in San Francisco, bridges throughout California, and the Union Oil Center in Los Angeles. It was while working at Independent Iron Works that Jim met the lovely Sharon Bounds (Cal class of ‘58). They were married in August 1960 at St. Leo’s Church in Oakland. In 1967, Jim and Sharon and the three boys moved to Piedmont where Jim resided the rest of his life. After the closure of Independent Iron Works in 1960, Jim’s entrepreneurship targeted specialized drayage services for numerous projects in the Bay Area and Northern California. Jim was a fixture at his company, Allied Crane and Rigging, through 2001, personally operating large cranes for construction projects. Jim had a generous disposiJim and Sharon Meagher enjoying the Oktoberfest in Germany in May 1971. Jim Meagher, a resident of Piedmont for 57 years, passed away in September 2024 at age 98. tion, a warm smile, and boundless energy to work and help others. With his three sons Jim became a dedicated Scouter, traveling on many trips and mentoring youth along the way. Scouting became a passion for Jim, and his years of dedication as Scoutmaster and Council member encompassed the Scouting experience. These included: National Jamboree, Woodbadge, Order of the Arrow, The Christmas Tree Lot and many 4th of July Parades. In honor of his impact on the lives of the youth in Piedmont, Jim received the Silver Beaver Award in 1987, Scouting’s highest award for volunteer leaders. It is not well known that among Jim’s other volunteer efforts he was an 18-year veteran of the Alameda County Deputy Sheriff’s Reserve (1966- 1984), where he won a handful of trophies as a sharpshooter. As a young man living on San Francisco’s Nob Hill, Jim was an equestrian and played polo in Golden Gate Park. Jim would tell colorful stories of his adventures, including flying to Pasadena to watch Cal in the 1959 Rose Bowl. In the mid-1950’s, Jim joined the family business and led notable projects for Independent Iron Works, including the James Lick Freeway in San Francisco, bridges throughout California, and the Union Oil Center in Los Angeles. It was while working at Independent Iron Works that Jim met the lovely Sharon Bounds (Cal class of ‘58). They were married in August 1960 at St. Leo’s Church in Oakland. In 1967, Jim and Sharon and the three boys moved to Piedmont where Jim resided the rest of his life. MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate Our greatest and most immediate challenge is to create a longterm, sustainable financial plan which allows Piedmont Unified to deliver exceptional academic outcomes, while simultaneously making it a great place to work for the District’s employees. We’re blessed with a community that continues to donate millions of dollars every year to subsidize our schools, in addition to the District’s sizeable school parcel taxes. This will become even more challenging as the schoolaged population continues to decline, and our pension liabilities continue to increase. We must reimagine how we prepare PUSD graduates for success in a rapidly changing workplace. As we do so, we must also land on a sustainable model, which encompasses the needs of students, District staff, and ultimately, the exceptional education Piedmont is known for. Turnover is high in nearly every profession, and our District is no exception. We’ll need to take a beginner’s mindset, and have the courage to incorporate new tools, approaches, and methodologies to achieve desired outcomes.
